slides.lead: Your newborn already knows your voice.
slides.sub: Under three days old, and already working to hear you over a stranger. A 1980 study in Science.

figure.label: babies under three days old chose their mother's voice

slides.head: The setup
slides.body:
Ten babies, all under three days old, sucked on a pacifier wired to a tape player.

Suck in one rhythm and they heard their mother reading a Dr. Seuss story. Suck in another and they heard a stranger reading the same story.

slides.head: What they did

stat.label: changed the timing of their sucking to keep their mother's voice playing

slides.body: With at most twelve hours of contact since birth. Sign test, p = .02.

slides.head: The catch
slides.body:
Ten babies is a small study, and the effect was found with one method in one lab.

What makes it hold up: later work found newborns prefer a story their mother read aloud before birth, and fetuses respond to her voice with measurable heart-rate changes.

slides.head: Why so fast
slides.body:
A baby has been hearing your muffled voice through the last trimester. By birth it is already the most familiar sound in the world.

Which is why ordinary talking, reading aloud and singing matter more than they seem to. You are not introducing yourself. You are continuing.
